newsitem.title: FRANCE: Unions urge Renault to keep Belgian plant open.
newsitem.headline: Unions urge Renault to keep Belgian plant open.

text.p: Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer held talks on Wednesday with union leaders eager to save 3,100 jobs at a Belgian plant the loss-making company has vowed to shut down.

Schweitzer and about 10 union officials met on "neutral ground" in Beauvais, a northern French city roughly midway between Renault's Paris headquarters and the plant at Vilvoorde which Renault has said it will shut down by July 27.
The negotiators said they would brief reporters after a two-hour meeting that began just after 3 p.m. (1400 GMT).
Union leaders said as they arrived that they opposed the shutdown and would seek to keep the plant open. "We're trying to be optimistic," Renault works council spokesman Karel Gacoms said.
Schweitzer had no comment as he entered the meeting.
Renault's case will be bolstered by an earnings report due out on Thursday expected to show more than 4.5 billion francs in losses for 1996, the firm's first annual losses in 10 years.

Despite a spate of boss-napping in France by angry workers, Renault said it was not worried about Schweitzer's safety. "Belgian trade unionists have always behaved themselves," a company spokeswoman said.
Nonetheless, main roads into the city were barred and French riot police surrounded the meeting site at the chamber of commerce building.
The Renault spokeswoman reaffirmed the carmaker considered its decision to close the plant to be "irrevocable" but would not say whether it was flexible on the July 27 deadline.
"They are meeting to discuss the closing of the Vilvoorde plant. There is no question of our changing our mind. They are going to discuss implementation," she told Reuters.
Union leaders said they planned initially to ask Schweitzer to back down and keep the plant open by an across-the-board cut in working hours at Renault.
Gacoms said enough work could be found to keep Vilvoorde's employees busy by trimming the hours at Renault plants across Europe by 10 percent.

Renault has said the main purpose for the shutdown is to streamline its car assembly operations in Europe. The car division has been losing money since the second half of 1995. Schweitzer said Renault's operations were too dispersed among plants that are much smaller than those of its rivals.
The company's performance deteriorated last year, when a downturn in the U.S. and European truck industries drove its commercial vehicle business into the red as well.
Analysts estimate Renault will show a loss of more than 4.5 billion francs for 1996, including a 2.4 billion franc charge to pay for the closure of the Belgian plant.
If Renault insists on the shutdown, union leaders said they would ask Schweitzer to keep it open until it finds a buyer.
One possible buyer might be Toyota, which has been studying the feasibility of a new plant in Europe.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene on Tuesday urged Schweitzer to consider the unions' proposals. He said they want to keep the plant open, after a restructuring, for two to three years during which a final solution could be worked out.
He said early retirement and shorter working weeks with a cut in social charges could be applied in the restructuring.
Renault's decision to close the plant has triggered outrage across Europe but particularly in Belgium where trade unions denounced the shock announcement as "unbelievably brutal".

French President Jacques Chirac has said he disapproved of the way the move was handled but acknowledged that plant closures "are, alas, part of life". The French state is the largest shareholder in Renault, with 46 percent.
The high-cost facility in Vilvoorde assembles Megane and Clio models. Renault said its output could be matched by the equivalent of 1,900 jobs at other, more efficient plants.
